readerTitle: The candy shop that paid for an empire
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Berkshire Hathaway, See's Candies) + 가상 적용 (B2B 급여 소프트웨어 회사)
insight: 최고의 사업은 돈을 많이 버는 사업이 아니라 성장에 돈이 거의 들지 않아 번 돈을 더 좋은 곳으로 옮길 수 있게 해 주는 사업이다.
misconception: 좋은 사업이 번 이익은 그 사업에 다시 쏟아부어야 한다. 장부가치보다 비싸게 사면 손해다.

sources.text: Berkshire Hathaway 2007 Shareholder Letter (See's: 1972 sales $30M, pretax < $5M, capital $8M; 2007 sales $383M, pretax $82M, capital $40M; $1.35B pretax earned, $32M reinvested, rest sent to Berkshire; 'great, good, gruesome')
Berkshire Hathaway 1983 Shareholder Letter, appendix on goodwill (purchase for $25M via Blue Chip Stamps; about $8M net tangible assets; about $2M after-tax earnings)

factChecks.note: 1972년 인수 가격 $25M, 순유형자산 약 $8M, 세후이익 약 $2M은 1983년 주주서한 부록에서 확인하세요. 인수 주체는 Berkshire가 지배하던 Blue Chip Stamps였습니다.
1972년 vs 2007년 수치(매출 $30M→$383M, 세전이익 <$5M→$82M, 필요 자본 $8M→$40M, 누적 세전이익 $1.35B, 재투자 $32M)는 2007년 주주서한 원문과 대조하세요.
계산: $25M ÷ $8M ≈ 3.1배("about three times"). $2M ÷ $8M = 25%. 세전이익 증가분은 $82M − 5M 미만 = 최소 $77M 이상. 재투자 $40M − $8M = $32M.
See's가 서부 지역 밖으로 크게 확장하는 데 어려움을 겪었다는 점은 Buffett 서한에 언급된 것으로 알려져 있으나 정확한 문구와 연도를 확인하세요. 카드에는 정성적으로만 적었습니다.
B2B 급여 소프트웨어 회사 사례와 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시입니다.

cards.title: The candy shop that paid for an empire
body: In 1972, Warren Buffett's group paid $25 million for See's Candies, a West Coast chocolate maker.
The business barely grew in size. Yet over the next decades it sent well over a billion dollars back to its owner. The secret wasn't the candy. It was where the money went next.

image.label: A box of chocolates with cash flowing out of it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 흰색 초콜릿 상자가 열려 있고, 상자에서 동전과 지폐가 강물처럼 흘러나와 화면 밖 여러 건물 방향으로 흘러감. 실제 See's 로고, 상자 디자인, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Would you pay three times what's on the books?
body: See's runs on about $8 million of assets: kitchens, shops, equipment. It earns about $2 million a year after tax. Customers love the brand and buy it as gifts every holiday.
The sellers want $25 million, about three times those assets. What do you do?

options.text: Pass. Paying triple the asset value is reckless
options.feedback: You avoid overpaying for the assets, but you miss what the price buys: a brand that earns 25% a year on what it uses.

options.text: Buy, if the brand can keep raising prices without needing much new money
options.feedback: You pay up front for a high return on little capital. The risk is that the brand fades, so this bet rests on loyal customers.

options.text: Offer only the $8 million asset value
options.feedback: A disciplined instinct, but the sellers know what the brand earns. You'd likely keep your cash and lose the deal.

cards.title: 35 years later, in Buffett's own numbers.
body: From 1972 to 2007, See's earned **$1.35 billion** before tax. It needed only $32 million of that to grow. Everything else went to Berkshire.

cards.title: Profit doesn't have to stay where it was made.
body: **Capital allocation** is deciding where each dollar of profit goes next. See's shows its quiet half: a great business earns a lot on the money it uses and needs little more to grow.
So the owner faces a choice. Force extra money into candy, where it can't earn much, or move it somewhere that can. Buffett chose to move it, and used See's cash to buy other businesses.

image.label: Small reinvestment arrow, large arrow out to other businesses
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 사탕 가게 아이콘. 작은 화살표 하나가 가게로 되돌아가고("$32M reinvested"), 굵은 화살표가 오른쪽 여러 회사 아이콘으로 뻗어 나감("The rest, to new businesses"). 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Great, good and gruesome.
body: In his 2007 letter, Buffett sorted businesses into three kinds.

Then he put the pieces together. See's could raise prices because people bought it as a treat or a gift, not to save money. Its shops didn't need to multiply. So each year its cash was free for whatever looked best across Berkshire.
list: **Great:** high returns, little new money needed to grow. See's.
**Good:** decent returns, but growth eats lots of new capital.
**Gruesome:** grows fast, needs heaps of capital, earns little. He named airlines.

cards.title: This only works under real conditions.
body: The brand must hold. Paying three times the assets made sense only because customers kept coming back at higher prices. A fading brand turns that premium into a loss.
You need better places to send the money. Moving cash out helps only if the new home earns more.
And don't starve a business that *can* grow well. See's reportedly struggled to expand far beyond its home market, so sending cash elsewhere was right. Another business might deserve the money.
cards.softwareNote: Many software products look like See's: once built, they need little new capital per extra customer. The same question applies. If growth needs only a little reinvestment, where should the rest of the cash go?

cards.title: Now it's a payroll software firm.
body: Your small B2B payroll software company earns $1 million a year. Clients rarely leave, and serving more of them costs little. Your team thinks a new office in another city would add only a few clients.
Meanwhile, a nearby bookkeeping firm with steady profits is for sale. What do you do with this year's profit?

options.text: Put it all into the new office. Profit belongs to the business that earned it
options.feedback: Loyal, but you push money into a project expected to earn little. That's the trap See's avoided.

options.text: Fund what the product truly needs, then weigh the bookkeeping firm against simply paying it out
options.feedback: You keep the core healthy and send the rest where it earns most. The cost is real work: judging a business you don't yet run.

options.text: Keep it all in the bank until a perfect idea appears
options.feedback: Safe and flexible, but idle cash earns little. Waiting is a choice too, so give it a deadline.

cards.title: A great business is one that frees its cash.
body: See's mattered less for how much it grew and more for how little money growth required. That freed cash built Berkshire.
**Try it today:** for your business, write down how much of last year's profit growth truly needed. Then ask where the rest would earn the most.
